standard.title: Language varies by context
standard.description: investigate how interpersonal language choices vary depending on the context, including the different roles taken on in interactions
standard.prior_knowledge: Students understand how language, facial expressions and gestures are used in different types of interaction (AC9E1LA01). They have not yet investigated how language choices vary systematically by context and by the roles participants take on.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can investigate how interpersonal language choices vary depending on context and the roles taken on in interactions, including culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness.

nodes.label: Context shapes language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that the same idea can be expressed using different language depending on who is speaking and who is listening.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples where language changes depending on the situation — e.g. greeting a friend vs greeting a teacher.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and discuss how language choices change across multiple everyday contexts — formal and informal, familiar and unfamiliar — and name what makes those contexts different.
wider: Compare greetings and expressions of politeness used in different cultural settings, including school, home and community contexts
Explore how digital communication contexts (e.g. text message vs formal letter) create different language expectations

response_modes.reason: Students often treat language as fixed — 'you just say what you mean'. Exposure to multiple contrasting contexts helps break the assumption that language is context-neutral. More examples across varied settings (not more explanation of one example) resolves this misconception.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: This foundational node is genuinely enriched by breadth — every new context (home, school, sport, digital) that students examine adds to their understanding of what 'context' means. First Nations cultural protocols offer a particularly rich example of how context shapes language.
success_criteria: Student can name at least one way their language would differ between a formal and informal context.
Student can explain what feature of the context causes the language to change (e.g. who they are talking to, the setting, the purpose).

nodes.label: Roles in interaction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how the role a person takes on in an interaction — speaker, listener, questioner, responder — influences their language choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify how a speaker's language changes when they take on different roles in the same interaction (e.g. asking a question vs giving an answer).
nodes.typical_width: Discuss how multiple roles in an interaction (leader, questioner, responder, instruction-giver) each carry different language expectations, and identify examples from classroom and familiar texts.
wider: Investigate roles in formal ceremony contexts such as First Nations Australian Welcome to Country, where the role of greeter, guest and witness carry distinct language protocols
Compare teacher–student and student–student interaction patterns, noting how the same student shifts language depending on their role
success_criteria: Student can identify at least two different roles in a given interaction and describe how the language differs for each.
Student can explain why a person speaking in one role would not use the same language as someone in a different role.

nodes.label: Familiarity and formality
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate how the degree of familiarity between participants affects language formality and vocabulary choices.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare language used with a familiar person (friend, family member) vs an unfamiliar person (new adult, community member) and name a difference.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how familiarity influences word choice, tone and degree of formality across multiple pairs of contrasting contexts, including culturally specific greetings and expressions of politeness.
wider: Identify First Nations Australian greeting words and protocols used with different groups — community members, visitors, Elders — and discuss how familiarity and respect shape these choices
Compare formal and informal email or spoken message openings to a known vs unknown audience, noting vocabulary and register differences

response_modes.reason: Students often conflate familiarity with friendship and assume formal language is 'cold'. Multiple cultural and social contexts help reveal that formality is a marker of respect, not distance — a misconception that widening directly addresses.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations Australian cultural protocols offer genuinely rich content here — Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country protocols are context-specific and role-specific in ways that make the familiarity-formality relationship vivid. This is a meaningful enrichment direction, not just more examples.
success_criteria: Student can give an example of a language choice they would make differently with a familiar vs unfamiliar person.
Student can explain what familiarity means in this context and how it influences language.
